summary: German-market conventions. Applications are usually made with a Lebenslauf, often alongside a cover letter (Anschreiben) and certificates (Zeugnisse).

photo.note: A professional photo is still common on German CVs, but omitting it is widely accepted and is a reasonable default for international applicants. Never required by law.

personalInfo.note: Some German employers still expect date of birth and nationality, but they are not required and their absence is not a legal ground for rejection. They stay hidden until you enable them.

page.note: Two pages is the norm for experienced candidates. A one-page Lebenslauf is acceptable early in a career.

notes: Large employers and staffing agencies increasingly parse applications automatically; a single-column, photo-free version is the safer choice for those pipelines.
Certificates are frequently requested as separate attachments rather than as CV sections.
German applications are typically written in the formal register (Sie), even when the advert is informal.
If the advert is published in English, an English CV is normally acceptable — this app offers both.

advisories.text: German employers often expect copies of degrees and employment references as separate attachments.
A handwritten or digital signature with place and date at the end of the CV is a long-standing convention. It is optional and increasingly omitted.
Long unexplained gaps in a German CV attract more attention than in most markets; a short factual note in the relevant entry is usually enough.
